rq3_entries.value: the tool transforms a selected paper implication into action wording, detailed guidance, contextual imagery, a paper summary, retrieved evidence, a citation, and a two-sided presentation (PDF p. 6).
quotes: "We also implemented a pipeline to automatically generate design cards from academic papers, which we discuss below." (p. 6)
"Specifically, we put core design card components (i.e., title, description, image) on the front side, and all the other components (i.e., paper summary, evidence, citation) on the backside." (p. 6)

rq3_entries.value: the initiating user still supplies the paper and selects the design-implication text to transform (PDF p. 6).
quotes: "Our system is implemented as a web interface, where the user can upload a paper PDF and choose the design implication text from which to generate a design card." (p. 6)

rq3_entries.value: the user must select the source and implication, and the designer must interpret whether and how to use the card; the paper describes no competence-based reduction in either responsibility (PDF p. 6).
quotes: "Our system is implemented as a web interface, where the user can upload a paper PDF and choose the design implication text from which to generate a design card." (p. 6)

rq3_entries.value: single_session (1) — both reported exposures were one-time sessions: a 45-minute preliminary interview and one online survey evaluating two papers (PDF pp. 4, 7).
quotes: "Each interview lasted approximately 45 minutes." (p. 4)
"Each participant in our study conducted a survey in our online survey interface." (p. 7)

claim_entries.value: designers perceived generated cards as more inspiring and generative than source-paper text, while paper authors regarded the system as an effective way to communicate their implications (PDF p. 1).
quotes: "Our evaluation with designers (𝑁 = 21) and authors of selected papers (𝑁 = 12) revealed that designers perceived the design implications from our design cards as more inspiring and generative, compared to reading original paper texts, and the authors viewed our system as an effective way of communicating their design implications." (p. 1)

claim_entries.value: within_subject — the main designer evaluation compared card and raw-text formats within participants; a preliminary interview and author email survey supplied additional qualitative evidence (PDF pp. 7–8).
quotes: "In order to understand the perception of designers toward the design cards generated by our system, we set up a within-subjects survey study with designers as follows:" (p. 7)

"To understand if our system can be an effective tool for the paper authors to communicate design implications, we contacted the authors of HCI papers asking them several open-ended questions via email." (p. 8)

claim_entries.value: 33 — 21 designers and 12 paper authors in the final evaluation (PDF p. 7).
quotes: "To evaluate the feasibility of communicating design implications using design cards generated by our system, we conducted a survey study with designers (𝑁 = 21) and authors of HCI papers (𝑁 = 12)." (p. 7)

claim_entries.value: mixed — working designers, design students, and HCI paper authors (PDF pp. 7–8).
quotes: "As a result, 21 designers completed the survey—13 were working as designers, 7 were pursuing a degree in design, and 1 was unemployed." (p. 7)
"We received responses from the authors of 12 papers in total, including from the authors of all 4 papers that were used for the survey study with designers, as well as 8 other respondents." (p. 8)

claim_entries.value: control_condition — raw source text versus the generated card for each selected paper (PDF p. 7).
quotes: "Each participant was asked to evaluate two papers that were randomly chosen, and for each paper, was presented two formats for communicating the design implication: (i) raw text format (a part of the paper that contains a design implication) and (ii) design card format." (p. 7)

claim_entries.value: test_only — linear mixed-effects tests with means, standard deviations, t statistics, and p values, but no effect sizes (PDF p. 8).
quotes: "The analysis revealed that there was a significant difference in the perception of inspirability (𝑡 = 3.53, 𝑝 < 0.001) and a marginally significant difference in the perception of generativity (𝑡 = 1.74, 𝑝 < 0.1)." (p. 8)

claim_entries.value: not reported for the final surveys; the preliminary interview lasted approximately 45 minutes (PDF p. 4).
quotes: "Each interview lasted approximately 45 minutes." (p. 4)

claim_entries.value: cards did not significantly change validity, generalizability, originality, or actionability; authors also identified incomplete or misleading evidence and image-to-intent misalignment (PDF pp. 8–10).
quotes: "There was also no significant difference in actionability between design cards and raw texts (𝑀 = 4.55, 𝑆𝐷 = 1.76 vs. 𝑀 = 4.38, 𝑆𝐷 = 1.79; 𝑡 = 0.48, 𝑝 = 0.63)." (p. 8)

"Yet, four authors mentioned that the evidence included in the design card of their paper could be potentially enhanced, by pointing out that it was partially correct, not the only evidence present in the paper, or misleading:" (p. 9)

"Despite the generally positive perceptions towards the generated images, a few authors did note some misalignment between their expectations toward the image representation and the actual image (e.g., Figure 5-b, c)." (p. 10)

claim_entries.value: the perception-scoped claim matches the within-subject format comparison and author feedback; it does not establish effects on real design work, which the authors explicitly leave untested (PDF pp. 8, 11).
quotes: "The linear mixed-effects modeling of our survey results revealed that designers perceived the content from the design card format as more inspiring (𝑀 = 5.21, 𝑆𝐷 = 1.22) and generative (𝑀 = 4.60, 𝑆𝐷 = 1.17), compared to the raw text format (𝑀 = 4.33, 𝑆𝐷 = 1.75; 𝑀 = 4.14, 𝑆𝐷 = 1.42) (Figure 4)." (p. 8)

"First, although we evaluated the qualities of design cards generated by our system, we did not test how generated design cards would be used in the real-world designing contexts of designers." (p. 11)

paper_code_entries.value: research-to-practice translation of HCI design implications — (PDF p. 1).
quotes: "This has led to several calls to develop better translational resources to bridge the gap between research and practice [21, 23]." (p. 1)

paper_code_entries.value: immediate_performance_or_sensemaking — the cards help designers consume and use research insights during design work (PDF p. 1).
quotes: "One solution is to use design cards as a form of translational resource that communicates valuable insights from papers in a more digestible and accessible format to assist in design processes." (p. 1)

paper_code_entries.value: mixed_or_transitioning — the evaluated readers included working designers and people pursuing design degrees (PDF p. 7).
quotes: "As a result, 21 designers completed the survey—13 were working as designers, 7 were pursuing a degree in design, and 1 was unemployed." (p. 7)

paper_code_entries.value: knowledge_or_concept_gap — jargon-heavy academic papers impede designers' access to relevant design knowledge (PDF p. 1).
quotes: "Designers describe difficulties reading the often jargon-filled papers and not finding academic papers useful [21]." (p. 1)

paper_code_entries.value: process — participants reported which format they preferred for consuming implications (PDF p. 8).
quotes: "In the survey results, 15 designers responded that they preferred to consume design implications using a design card format, while 3 preferred the raw text format; the other 3 designers had no preference." (p. 8)

paper_code_entries.value: artifact — the study measured perceived qualities of the card-presented implication (PDF p. 8).
quotes: "The linear mixed-effects modeling of our survey results revealed that designers perceived the content from the design card format as more inspiring (𝑀 = 5.21, 𝑆𝐷 = 1.22) and generative (𝑀 = 4.60, 𝑆𝐷 = 1.17), compared to the raw text format (𝑀 = 4.33, 𝑆𝐷 = 1.75; 𝑀 = 4.14, 𝑆𝐷 = 1.42) (Figure 4)." (p. 8)

paper_code_entries.value: structuring — the card separates key guidance from optional background through a visible hierarchy (PDF p. 8).
quotes: "Participants reported the card format to be well-structured, with a clear visual hierarchy that facilitated information processing." (p. 8)

paper_code_entries.value: hybrid_or_multi_model — an LLM generates textual meaning and prompts a separate text-to-image model for the visual meaning (PDF p. 7).
quotes: "For the system implementation tested in our evaluation, we used GPT-3 as our LLM for generating all textual components, and DALL-E 2 for images." (p. 7)

paper_code_entries.value: llm_era — the scaffold's content is generated through GPT-3 plus a text-to-image model (PDF p. 7).
quotes: "For the system implementation tested in our evaluation, we used GPT-3 as our LLM for generating all textual components, and DALL-E 2 for images." (p. 7)

limitations: "However, our survey with paper authors revealed that extracted evidence for a design implication can sometimes be inaccurate or not perfectly aligned with the part of the paper authors used to derive the design implication." (PDF p. 11)

"Despite the efficacy of AI-generated images in providing an overall context of the design implication, a few authors from our study reported a misalignment between the card images and their expectations based on their original intent (e.g., unintended emotion of the depicted user), or expressed a wish to include a representative figure directly from the paper to further help readers’ understanding." (PDF p. 11)
"Although we designed our title to involve action, our survey with designers revealed no significant difference in actionability between the design card format and raw text format." (PDF p. 11)

"First, although we evaluated the qualities of design cards generated by our system, we did not test how generated design cards would be used in the real-world designing contexts of designers." (PDF p. 11)
"Our interface also assumes a context where the paper segments containing design implications need to be manually localized." (PDF p. 11)

"Additionally, although our focus was to demonstrate the potential of AI-generated cards by choosing reasonable methods, there are many alternate models, techniques, and prompts that could be used to build our system." (PDF p. 11)

"Similarly, although our characterization of design card components was based on our cursory examination of existing design card sets, there may also exist alternative design components to achieve our goal of creating useful translational resources for designers (e.g., including different card elements for inspirational purposes)." (PDF p. 11)

"As utilizing AI-generated images may retain biases from the datasets they are trained on, it is an open concern [13, 49] that the outputs manifest gender and racial stereotypes (e.g., higher likelihood of featuring white men rather than representative users; negative associations for certain racial/ethnic groups)." (PDF p. 11)
boundary_conditions: "Regarding the target audience for our system and the generated artifact, we intended the generated design cards to be specifically read and consumed by designers." (PDF p. 11)
"To test our hypothesis, we develop and evaluate an end-to-end system to automatically generate design cards from HCI publications." (PDF p. 1)
"Our interface also assumes a context where the paper segments containing design implications need to be manually localized." (PDF p. 11)
cards.notes: - The empirical contribution combines a preliminary interview, a within-subjects designer survey, and an author email survey, but `study_design` permits one token. Coded `within_subject` for the main controlled comparison, which loses the other two designs.
